questions.stem: What are the three components of a DNA nucleotide?
options: A phosphate group, ribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
An amino acid, deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, glucose sugar and a long fatty acid chain
A phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
questions.explanation: Each DNA nucleotide has a phosphate group, the five-carbon sugar deoxyribose and one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine, thymine, guanine or cytosine. Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 18% adenine. What percentage of its bases are cytosine?
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine, so thymine is also 18%, and A + T = 36%. The remaining 64% is shared equally by guanine and cytosine, so cytosine is 32%. The value 64% forgets to split G + C between the two bases.

questions.stem: Why must a DNA molecule rich in guanine-cytosine pairs be heated to a higher temperature to separate its two strands?
options: G-C pairs are joined by two hydrogen bonds, but A-T pairs by three
G-C pairs lie in the sugar-phosphate backbone, unlike the A-T pairs
G-C pairs are joined by three hydrogen bonds, but A-T pairs by only two
G-C pairs are joined by covalent bonds, but A-T pairs by hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: three between G and C, two between A and T. More G-C pairs means more hydrogen bonds to break. The bonds between paired bases are hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.

questions.stem: One strand of DNA reads 5' ATGCCA 3'. What is the sequence of its complementary strand?
options: 3' GCATTG 5'
3' TACGGT 5'
3' UACGGU 5'
3' ATGCCA 5'
questions.explanation: A pairs with T and G pairs with C, and the complementary strand runs in the opposite direction, so it reads 3' TACGGT 5'. Uracil is found in RNA, not DNA.

questions.stem: A eukaryotic gene is about 12 000 base pairs long, but the mature mRNA made from it is only about 2000 nucleotides long. What best explains the difference?
options: Most of the gene is introns, which are removed before the mRNA is used
Most of the gene is exons, which are removed before the mRNA is used
Only one strand is transcribed, so the mRNA is half of the gene's length
The promoter region makes up most of the gene and is not transcribed
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic genes contain introns, non-coding sequences that are transcribed into pre-mRNA and then spliced out, leaving the exons joined in the mature mRNA. Exons are the sequences kept. One strand is transcribed, but that would not by itself shorten the mRNA to one-sixth.

questions.stem: What are sister chromatids?
options: Two different chromosomes that exchange segments during a translocation
Two identical copies of one chromosome, joined at the centromere after replication
A pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, carrying the genes for the same traits
The two strands of a DNA double helix, held together by hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: When a chromosome is replicated, the two identical copies stay joined at the centromere as sister chromatids until they separate. A pair of chromosomes with one from each parent is a homologous pair.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a pair of homologous chromosomes?
options: They carry the same alleles as each other, but at different gene loci
They carry the same genes at the same loci, but may carry different alleles
They carry identical alleles at every locus, because they are exact copies of each other
They carry different genes at the same loci, one gene from each parent
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes, one maternal and one paternal, carry the same genes in the same order, each at its locus. The alleles at a locus can be the same or different. Identical copies of one chromosome are sister chromatids, not homologues.

questions.stem: What are telomeres?
options: Small circular DNA molecules that are found in bacterial cells
Repeated non-coding sequences that protect the ends of chromosomes
The constricted regions where sister chromatids are held together
Proteins around which DNA is wound to package it in the nucleus
questions.explanation: Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences at the ends of linear chromosomes that protect the coding DNA from being lost or damaged. The centromere joins sister chromatids, histones package DNA, and small circular DNA molecules in bacteria are plasmids.

questions.stem: Which feature is found in the DNA of a bacterium but not in the nuclear DNA of a human cell?
options: Linear chromosomes capped by telomeres
DNA wound around histones in a nucleus
Genes containing many long introns
A circular chromosome, often with plasmids
questions.explanation: Bacteria have a single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm and often extra small circular plasmids. Linear chromosomes with telomeres, packaging around histones in a nucleus and genes with many introns are features of eukaryotic nuclear DNA.

questions.stem: Apart from the nucleus, where is DNA found in a plant leaf cell?
options: In the cell wall and the vacuole, as linear chromosomes
In the cell membrane, as small linear chromosomes
In the mitochondria and chloroplasts, as circular DNA
In the ribosomes and Golgi apparatus, as circular DNA
questions.explanation: Mitochondria and chloroplasts each contain their own small circular DNA molecules, like those of prokaryotes. Ribosomes contain RNA and protein, and the cell wall and vacuole contain no chromosomes.

questions.stem: What is the role of helicase in DNA replication?
options: It unwinds the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between bases
It adds new nucleotides one at a time to the 3' end of the growing strand
It joins Okazaki fragments together on the lagging strand
It removes introns from the newly replicated DNA molecule
questions.explanation: Helicase separates the two strands by breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, so each strand can act as a template. DNA polymerase adds the nucleotides, and DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments.

questions.stem: Why is one strand of DNA, the lagging strand, copied as a series of short Okazaki fragments?
options: The lagging strand contains introns, which must be skipped as the strand is being copied
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to a 5' end, so it copies that strand in reverse
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to a 3' end, so it works away from the fork on that strand
Helicase can unwind only short sections of that strand before the strand rejoins its partner
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase builds new DNA only in the 5' to 3' direction, adding to a 3' end. On one template strand this direction runs towards the replication fork, so synthesis is continuous; on the other it runs away from the fork, so short fragments are made and later joined.

questions.stem: Which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments into a continuous strand?
options: RNA polymerase
A restriction enzyme
DNA ligase
Helicase
questions.explanation: DNA ligase forms bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone between adjacent fragments, making one continuous strand. Helicase unwinds the helix, and restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences.

questions.stem: Bacteria grown for many generations with heavy nitrogen-15 are moved to medium with only light nitrogen-14 and allowed to replicate their DNA twice. What DNA is present after the second replication?
options: All hybrid, with one heavy strand and one light strand in each
Half fully heavy and half fully light, with no hybrid molecules
One quarter fully heavy, one half hybrid and one quarter light
Half hybrid (one heavy and one light strand) and half fully light
questions.explanation: Replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule keeps one parent strand. After one round every molecule is hybrid. In the second round each hybrid gives one hybrid and one fully light molecule, so half are hybrid and half light. No fully heavy molecules remain after the first round.

questions.stem: What is a point mutation?
options: A change in the number of whole chromosomes in a cell
The reversal of a large segment within a chromosome
The transfer of a segment to a non-homologous chromosome
A change to a single nucleotide in a DNA sequence
questions.explanation: A point mutation changes one nucleotide, usually by substitution of one base for another. Changes in chromosome number, inversions and translocations are chromosomal abnormalities affecting many genes.

questions.stem: Why does deleting one nucleotide near the start of a gene usually affect the protein more than substituting one nucleotide?
options: The deletion always creates a stop codon at the exact point of deletion
A substitution can never change the amino acid that a codon codes for
The deletion removes the promoter, so the gene is never transcribed
The deletion shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it
questions.explanation: mRNA is read in triplets, so losing one nucleotide shifts the reading frame and changes every codon downstream, usually giving a non-functional protein. A substitution changes at most one codon, and it can change the amino acid, so the claim that it never does is false.

questions.stem: Ultraviolet light can cause two adjacent thymine bases in DNA to bond to each other. Why does this make UV light a mutagen?
options: It causes non-disjunction, so cells gain an extra chromosome
If not repaired, the damage can cause errors when the DNA is replicated
It converts the thymine bases into uracil bases throughout the gene
It breaks every hydrogen bond in the DNA, so the strands separate
questions.explanation: The bonded thymines distort the helix. If the damage is not repaired, DNA polymerase may insert the wrong bases or skip bases during replication, producing point or frameshift mutations. Mutagens are physical or chemical factors that increase the mutation rate in this way.

questions.stem: Three adjacent nucleotides are deleted from the coding region of a gene. What is the most likely effect on the polypeptide?
options: Three amino acids are each replaced, but the length is unchanged
The polypeptide is unchanged, as three nucleotides is too few to matter
One amino acid is lost, but the reading frame after it is unchanged
Every amino acid after the deletion changes, as the frame has shifted
questions.explanation: Three nucleotides make one codon, so deleting three adjacent nucleotides removes one amino acid (or alters two adjacent ones if the deletion spans codons) while keeping the reading frame. Only insertions or deletions that are not a multiple of three cause frameshifts.

questions.stem: A plant has a diploid number of 6. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can it produce by independent assortment?
questions.explanation: With 3 homologous pairs, each pair can line up two ways, giving 2 to the power 3 = 8 combinations. The value 6 is the diploid number, and 64 would be 2 to the power 6, using the diploid rather than the haploid number.

questions.stem: At which stage of meiosis does independent assortment occur?
options: Metaphase II, when single chromosomes line up at the equator
Telophase II, when four haploid nuclei form around the separated chromatids
Metaphase I, when homologous pairs line up randomly at the equator
Prophase I, when homologous chromosomes exchange sections of DNA
questions.explanation: In metaphase I each homologous pair orients randomly, so which maternal and paternal chromosomes go to each pole is independent of the other pairs. Exchange of sections between homologues in prophase I is crossing over, a separate source of variation.

questions.stem: Ignoring crossing over, independent assortment lets each human produce about 8.4 million (2 to the power 23) chromosome combinations in gametes. Including random fertilisation, about how many combinations could a couple's child have?
options: About 8.4 million (2 to the power 23)
About 17 million (2 × 2 to the power 23)
About 46 (one for each chromosome)
About 70 trillion (2 to the power 46)
questions.explanation: Any one of about 8.4 million kinds of sperm could fuse with any one of about 8.4 million kinds of egg, so the possibilities multiply: 2 to the power 23 × 2 to the power 23 = 2 to the power 46, about 70 trillion. Adding the two numbers, giving 17 million, does not account for every pairing.

questions.stem: How many functional gametes are produced from one cell entering meiosis in spermatogenesis and in oogenesis?
options: Four sperm, but one egg and polar bodies
One sperm, but four eggs and no polar bodies
Four sperm, and four eggs and no polar bodies
Two sperm, but two eggs and one polar body
questions.explanation: A primary spermatocyte gives four functional sperm. A primary oocyte gives one egg, with the other products of meiosis forming small polar bodies that degenerate.

questions.stem: Why is the cytoplasm divided unequally during oogenesis?
options: So the egg keeps most of the cytoplasm and nutrients for the early embryo
So the polar bodies receive enough cytoplasm to develop into extra eggs later
So the egg is small enough to travel quickly through the oviduct
So each sperm that reaches the egg receives an equal share of cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Unequal division concentrates cytoplasm, organelles and stored nutrients in one large egg, which supports the zygote until it implants. Polar bodies receive very little cytoplasm and degenerate rather than becoming eggs.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the timing of spermatogenesis and oogenesis in humans?
options: Spermatogenesis runs continuously from puberty; oogenesis starts before birth and pauses
Oogenesis runs continuously from puberty; spermatogenesis starts before birth and pauses
Both processes start before birth and then run continuously throughout adult life
Both processes start at puberty and stop completely by the age of about fifty
questions.explanation: Sperm are produced continuously in large numbers from puberty. Oogenesis begins before birth, and primary oocytes pause in prophase I for years; meiosis resumes in one oocyte at a time from puberty.

questions.stem: At ovulation a secondary oocyte is released, paused partway through meiosis II. When does it complete meiosis II?
options: When the embryo implants
At the next menstruation
When a sperm fertilises it
As it enters the oviduct
questions.explanation: The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II and completes meiosis II only if a sperm penetrates it, producing the mature ovum and a second polar body. An unfertilised oocyte never completes meiosis II.

questions.stem: A segment of a chromosome breaks out and is reinserted the opposite way round. What is this abnormality?
options: A duplication
Aneuploidy
An inversion
A translocation
questions.explanation: An inversion reverses the order of genes in a segment of one chromosome. A translocation moves a segment to a non-homologous chromosome, a duplication repeats a segment, and aneuploidy is a change in the number of chromosomes.

questions.stem: A section breaks off chromosome 9 and becomes attached to chromosome 22, a non-homologous chromosome. What is this abnormality?
options: A duplication
A translocation
A deletion within chromosome 22
An inversion
questions.explanation: Moving a segment from one chromosome to a non-homologous chromosome is a translocation. An inversion keeps the segment on the same chromosome, reversed, and a duplication repeats a segment.

questions.stem: Homologous chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis I. What gametes result?
options: Gametes with every chromosome present as a single strand
Gametes with one extra or one missing chromosome
Gametes with a complete extra set of chromosomes
Gametes with the normal number but a reversed segment
questions.explanation: This failure, non-disjunction, sends both homologues to one pole, so the gametes have n + 1 or n − 1 chromosomes. Fertilisation then produces aneuploid zygotes, such as trisomies or monosomies.

questions.stem: During crossing over, two homologous chromatids misalign and exchange unequal lengths of DNA. What is the result?
options: Both chromatids are inverted, but keep all of their genes
One chromatid moves to a non-homologous chromosome
One chromatid gains a duplication and the other has a deletion
Both chromatids gain a duplication of the same length of DNA
questions.explanation: If the crossover points are not opposite each other, one chromatid receives an extra copy of a segment, a duplication, while its partner loses that segment, a deletion. No inversion or translocation is involved.

questions.stem: A person's karyotype shows 22 pairs of autosomes and a single X chromosome, with no second sex chromosome. Which condition is predicted?
options: Turner syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome
Down syndrome
Edwards syndrome
questions.explanation: A karyotype of 45,X, monosomy of the X chromosome, gives Turner syndrome. Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY, Down syndrome is trisomy 21 and Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18.

questions.stem: A karyotype from a fetus shows three copies of every chromosome, 69 in total. What has occurred?
options: Trisomy 21, an extra copy of chromosome 21 in every cell
Triploidy, a change in the number of whole chromosome sets
Aneuploidy, a change in the number of one chromosome only
A translocation, which joined extra sets onto chromosome 1
questions.explanation: Three complete sets (3n = 69) is triploidy, a change in ploidy affecting every chromosome. Aneuploidy, such as trisomy 21, changes the number of a single chromosome and gives 47 rather than 69.

questions.stem: Why are X-linked recessive disorders such as haemophilia much more common in males than in females?
options: Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed
Males have two X chromosomes, so they receive twice as many alleles
The Y chromosome carries a dominant allele that causes the disorder
Females cannot inherit X-linked alleles from their father at all
questions.explanation: Males are XY, so the one allele on their X chromosome is always expressed. Females have two X chromosomes and are affected only if both carry the recessive allele. Daughters do inherit their father's X chromosome.

questions.stem: In ABO blood groups, the alleles IA and IB are codominant and both are dominant to i. A person with group AB has children with a person with group O. What are the expected blood groups of the children?
options: Half group AB and half group O
All of the children group AB
A quarter each of A, B, AB and O
Half group A and half group B
questions.explanation: IA IB × ii gives offspring IA i, which are group A, and IB i, which are group B, in equal numbers. No child can be AB, because one parent gives only i, and none can be O, because every child gets IA or IB from the AB parent.

questions.stem: Rabbit coat colour has multiple alleles with dominance C > cch (chinchilla) > ch (Himalayan) > c (albino). A cch c rabbit is crossed with a ch c rabbit. What phenotype ratio is expected?
options: 1 chinchilla : 1 Himalayan : 1 albino
3 chinchilla : 1 albino, no Himalayan
2 chinchilla : 1 Himalayan : 1 albino
1 chinchilla : 2 Himalayan : 1 albino
questions.explanation: The offspring genotypes are cch ch, cch c, ch c and c c in equal numbers. The first two are chinchilla because cch is dominant to both ch and c, ch c is Himalayan, and c c is albino: 2 : 1 : 1.

questions.stem: A woman who carries the allele for red-green colour blindness (XB Xb) has children with a colour-blind man (Xb Y). What proportion of their daughters are expected to be colour-blind?
options: All of them
One half
One quarter
None
questions.explanation: Every daughter receives Xb from her father. From her mother she receives XB or Xb with equal chance, so half the daughters are Xb Xb and colour-blind and half are XB Xb carriers.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, two affected parents have an unaffected daughter. Which mode of inheritance best fits this?
options: X-linked dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Autosomal dominant
questions.explanation: Affected parents with an unaffected child means both parents are heterozygous for a dominant allele, so the trait is dominant. It cannot be X-linked dominant, because an affected father passes his X to every daughter, who would then be affected.

questions.stem: A pedigree shows a trait in many males but almost no females. Affected males usually have unaffected parents, and the trait is never passed from father to son. Which mode of inheritance best fits?
options: Y-linked
X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
Autosomal dominant
questions.explanation: Mostly affected males, transmission through unaffected carrier mothers and no father-to-son transmission fit X-linked recessive inheritance. A Y-linked trait would pass from every affected father to every son, and a dominant trait would usually appear in a parent.

questions.stem: Two parents who are both carriers of cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder, have an unaffected child. What is the probability that this child is a carrier?
questions.explanation: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff and ff in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio. The child is unaffected, so ff is ruled out, leaving three equally likely genotypes, two of which are carriers: 2/3. The value 1/2 counts carriers among all four outcomes.

questions.stem: Height in a population varies continuously, and a histogram of heights forms a bell-shaped curve. What does this suggest about how height is inherited?
options: It is X-linked, so males and females have separate height classes
It is controlled by one gene with three or more multiple alleles
It is polygenic, controlled by many genes plus environmental effects
It is controlled by one gene with a dominant and a recessive allele
questions.explanation: Many genes, each adding a small effect, together with environmental influences such as nutrition, give many phenotypes that merge into continuous variation. A single gene gives a few distinct classes rather than a smooth curve.

questions.stem: Kernel colour in wheat is crossed to an F2 generation, and a histogram shows five colour classes from white to dark red in the ratio 1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1. What is the best explanation?
options: One gene with five codominant alleles controls kernel colour
Four genes, each with additive alleles, control kernel colour
One gene with complete dominance and an environmental effect
Two genes, each with additive alleles, control kernel colour
questions.explanation: With additive polygenic inheritance, n genes give 2n + 1 phenotype classes, so five classes means two genes. The 1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1 ratio comes from counting 0 to 4 contributing alleles in a cross of AaBb × AaBb. Four genes would give nine classes.
